### Strength 4: Unique contributions in both confidence-guided gating mechanism and the two-stage imputation strategy. (Reviewer q3sb)

Standard softmax-based gating becomes unreliable under missing-modality conditions because it assigns disproportionately high routing scores even when the input representations are poor. This behavior amplifies expert collapse, as the router consistently activates the same experts regardless of input quality. ConfNet addresses this issue by directly grounding gating weights in downstream task confidence. When a modality is unreliable (e.g missing modality is considered as zero), its confidence is naturally low to ground label, leading the router to assign lower routing scores. This reduces the influence of corrupted or missing inputs and encourages the model to select alternative experts, resulting in more stable routing and balanced expert utilization without relying on auxiliary regularization losses.

In addition, our method incorporates a two-stage imputation strategy with ConfNet router that leverages complementary “expert opinions” to reconstruct missing modalities. Instead of depending on a single model’s reconstruction, ConfNet aggregates diverse expert outputs, enabling more accurate and robust imputation. This design yields higher reliability recovery of missing data and improved performance under incomplete multimodal inputs. Overall, ConfNet simultaneously mitigates expert collapse and enhances missing-modality reconstruction, providing a more resilient and effective multimodal MoE framework.




We thank that all reviewers identify the potential limitation of our proposed method and raise the concerns in discussion period. We believe all minor concerns such as typos, comparison with closely related gating approaches, parameter sensitivity and so on have been well-addressed. As we have provided further clarification and experimental results to address them. We would like to highlight some common concerns (Concern 1 \& 2) and one misunderstanding point (Concern 3) from Reviewer 8riB

### Conerns 1: Achitecture Complexity (Reviewer dEKy, 8riB, q3sb)

In discussion period, we comprehensively compare complexity of proposed method to the most competitive in different perspectives such as Train / Inference Time (ms/step), MFLOPs, #Parameter, and Train Average Memory. We listed the comparison as below:


We acknowledge that the pose-imputation can increase training cost under the same hyperparameter (e.g. number of layers, hidden size, number of head). However, the training time depends on many factors such as data parallel and programming efficiency. FlexMoE follows fastmoe library to accelerate MoE forward by data parallel, this is the reason that we show FLOPs as complexity metrics as this is gives actual operation counts on floating-point operations. Furthermore, we did not adapt our approach on fastmoe as it does not allow us to control the behavior of gating score and integrate with our post-imputation. Thus, we do not have any data parallel implementation in our intial implementation. Therefore, we show how much computational cost wtih and without post-imputation, and will revise our implementation to the data parallel version implementation afterward. We can still see that the post-computation indeed brings additional computational cost, but the complexity still remains at the same level as FuseMoE, which is acceptable for the performance gains.


| Metric | FuseMoE | FlexMoE | ConfNet w/ post-imputation | ConfNet w/o post-imputation|
| ------ | ---- |------- | ---- |------- |
| Train Time (ms / step) | 24  | 15  | 30  | 20  |

* **Q2: What is the sensitivity analysis of the sparsity hyperparameter (B) in post-imputation, i.e., Line 300 how sensitive is the model performance to hyperparameter T for top-T entry?**

    The sparsity hyperparameter in post-imputation determines the amount of feature retrieved from available modality and filtering out irrelavant feature from them. The higher the sparsity B is, the sparser the attention mechanism will be. The post-imputation module will be standard attention if $B=1$. In the paper, we keep $B=4$ as this is the best parameter we search in range [1, 7]. To show the sensitivity of B, we implemented experiment to evaluate how B hyperparameter impact the model performance as follow:

    | Dataset | Metric | B=1 | B=2 | B=3 | B=4 | B=5 | B=6 | B=7 |
    | ---- | ------ | ---- |------- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- |
    | CMU-MOSI-50%  | F1  | 44.71 $\pm$ 1.72 | 43.37 $\pm$ 1.41 | 43.13 $\pm$ 0.32 | 44.34 $\pm$ 0.77 | 43.33 $\pm$ 0.48 | 43.51 $\pm$ 0.71 | 43.19 $\pm$ 0.19 |
    |               | AUC | 69.33 $\pm$ 0.97 | 68.45 $\pm$ 0.57 | 69.45 $\pm$ 1.60 | 70.41 $\pm$ 1.31 | 69.77 $\pm$ 1.31 | 68.92 $\pm$ 1.15 | 68.12 $\pm$ 0.23 |

    Note: CMU-MOSI-50% represents CMU-MOSI dataset with 50% modality missing as in Experiment setting II.

    We can clearly see that $B=4$ is an optimal value to balance on filtering out irrelavant information and retrieve high quality information from available modality. An inapproriate selection of sparsity hyperparameter B can harm the performance.


* **Q3: Could the confidence gate improve MoE models without missing data?**
    
    Yes, we have provided experiment in Table 8, 9 in appendix. There is a 0\% missing rate setting for dataset CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI. The improvement of ConfNet still holds (0.3 - 1.8) over the second best baseline. It also shows improvement over the baseline and the improvement is statistically stable than others as we have smaller deviation on both F1 and AUC. This evidence should be able to support the effectiveness of the ConfNet. It is worthy to note that CMU-MOSEI is the extended version of CMU-MOSI with more samples. Our proposed method improves more than CMU-MOSI, showing stronger learning capability.

### Conern 3: Sparse MoE is not differentiable (Reviewer 8riB)


We noticed that Reviewer 8riB seems to have different opinion on whether Sparse MoE is differentiable. 


Reviewer 8riB believe that Sparse MoE is not differentiable due to the discontinuity of TopK function so as the validity of Jocibian of Sparse MoE will be doubtful (Eq.(2) as in original paper and Eq (3) as in revision paper). 


We argue that Sparse MoE is partially differentialble, in other word, we consider Sparse MoE is not fully differentiable but it is dfferentiable at where the expert is activated, given the fact that the TopK function can be condered as a constant binary mask. The discontinuity of TopK function does not neccesarily decide that Sparse MoE is not diffentiable and we show this in the following:


Denote that input token embedding $\mathbf{h} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and the a learnable softmax router $G(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{\text{exp}(u_i)}{\sum_j^d \text{exp}(u_{j})} = \mathbf{g} = [g_1, g_2, \dots, g_N]$, where $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{W_r} \mathbf{h}$ and $\mathbf{W_r} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$  is the weight of router to linearly map $\mathbf{h}$ to gating logits $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. $G(\mathbf{u})$ produces routing score $g_i$ for each expert $E_i$ from expert pool $\mathbf{E} = [E_1, E_2, \dots, E_N] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$. We consider the Top-K operation as a binary mask $\mathbf{m} \in \{0, 1\}^N$ to select the Top-K experts in forward as shown in the following:

$$
\mathbf{m} = \text{Top-K}(\mathbf{g}, K) = \mathbf{1}\{\text{if } g_i \text{ is in the top K element of } \mathbf{g} \} \quad \quad  \text{(1)}
$$


$$
E(\mathbf{h}) = \mathbf{h} + \sum^N_{i=1} m_i g_i E_i(\mathbf{h})  \quad \quad  \text{(2)}
$$


Therefore, we can take the Jacobian of Eq (2) as below


$$ \mathbf{J} = \sum^N_{i=1} m_i \frac{\partial g_i} {\partial \mathbf{h}} E_i(\mathbf{h}) + \sum^N_{i=1} m_i g_i E_i^{'}(\mathbf{h}) \quad \quad  \text{(3)} $$ 


Note that expert $E_i(\mathbf{h})$ and softmax gating $G(\mathbf{u})$ themselves are differentiable w.r.t $\mathbf{h}$ and the mask $\mathbf{m} = \text{Top-K}(\mathbf{g}, K)$ is a piecewise-constant mask that only changes when the ordering of routing score $\mathbf{g}$ changes. Conditioning on a fixed mask $\mathbf{m}$, The Eq. (2) reduces to a linear combination of differentiable functions, where the gradient will only propagate through the terms with $m_i=1$, enabling parameter update for those activated experts. Consequently, during training, only the selected experts are differentiable. With this description, it should be clear to show that Sparse MoE is partial differentiable at where the experts are activated.



### A little more to read
To show how TopK function can be used in calculating gradient and not causing any problem in practice as mentioned in [1], we would like to highlight that TopK has similar property as ReLU is a piecewise differentiable function: 

Consider a gating score $\mathbf{g} \in \mathbb{R}^N$, where $N$ is the number of expert.

>ReLU keeps value when $x > 0$ and others are zeros, while TopK keeps the top K values and others are zeros.

>ReLU is not differentiable at $x=0$ and TopK function is not differentiable at $g_K = g_{K+1}$, which means that the $K$-th and $K+1$-th value are the same value. TopK function has no idea which value to select. This leads to non-differentiable results.


However, $Pr(g_i = g_{i+1}) = 0$ when $g_i$ is a continuous distribution, the probability of two equal continuous value is zero. Note that the neural network and the gating function are all continuous as they are intialized as float number, then. Therefore, the non-differentiable point of TopK is a set of measure-zero, which the probability of occurrence is negligible. This conclusion is consistent with ReLU function, which the $x=0$ for a continuous neural network is a set of measure zero, $Pr(x=0) = 0$. 

To this point, we can claim that the Eq. (3) is valid, we believe this should be able to address the concern 3 and the misunderstanding of Reviwer 8riB.

[1] Noam Shazeer, Azalia Mirhoseini, Krzysztof Maziarz, Andy Davis, Quoc Le, Geoffrey Hinton, and Jeff Dean. Outrageously large neural networks: The sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer. In ICLR, 2017.

To be clear, we quote the original statment of [1] that stated the dis-continuity concerns:

We thank the Reviewer q3sb spending time and efforts to review our work and provide valuable comments. We wish the following reponse can address your concerns: 


**W1: Based on my understanding, the framework does not fully address temporal or causal dependencies among modalities or expert activations, which is a common problem in healthcare/activity monitoring/autonomous driving etc. The current design assumes static modality relationships and focuses primarily on handling missing inputs at the feature level. In dynamic settings such as time-evolving multimodal data or streaming environments, confidence-guided gating and two-stage imputation may not adapt quickly to changing modality relevance. So it is interesting to see further extension of this work on these settings.**

Thanks for bring this potential applicaiton to our attention, we acknowledge that this work assumes the modalities are static relationship. The time-evolving scenairo is still underexplore and we will put this into our limitation and future work. 



**W2: Although the two-stage imputation is effective in handling inter-modality relationships, it may introduce additional computational overhead and stochasticity into the model training procedure.**

The two-stage imputation indeed introduce additional computational cost. Thus, we fairly compare with other baseline by controling the complexity (e.g FLOPs and Parameter) under the same level and ours still outperform as shown in Table 14. 

**W3: In line 244, it is not very clear how the “token-level confidence” is computed or propagated through the MoE.**

We compute the confidence of each token $c_i$ w.r.t ground-truth label via ConfNet to replace with softmax gating score, we denote the variant using token-level confidence as ConfSMoE-T in our experiment. Token-level basically means each token itself has one confidence score to label as not all tokens are equally contributed to downstream task.

summary.value:
This paper proposes ConfSMoE, a confidence-guided sparse MoE framework that aims to jointly address expert collapse and missing-modality robustness via confidence-based routing and a two-stage imputation module. One reviewer (q3sb) is positive and views the contribution as meaningful, while two reviewers (dEKy and 8riB) are skeptical, mainly due to concerns about conceptual novelty and theoretical rigor.

After reading the paper and the discussion myself, I share many of the reservations raised by the reviewers. While the problem is timely and the empirical results are reasonably solid, the paper reads more like a careful engineering combination of known ideas than a clean conceptual advance. In particular, the link between confidence-guided routing and missing-modality imputation feels loosely motivated, and the imputation design itself is incremental relative to prior multimodal fusion and imputation work. More importantly, the theoretical analysis around Top-K routing and gradient flow is not presented with sufficient rigor, and the rebuttal does not fully resolve these issues. Given that these theoretical claims are used to justify the core design, this weakens the overall contribution. For these reasons, despite improvements in the rebuttal, I recommend rejection.

reviewer_concerns.value:
Concerns that remain unresolved or only partially resolved:

1. I agree with Reviewer dEKy that the paper combines two ideas (collapse mitigation and imputation) without a sufficiently strong conceptual unification. The two-stage imputation module is close to existing designs, and the overall novelty feels limited.

2. I align with Reviewer 8riB’s concern that the treatment of Top-K routing, differentiability, and the associated derivations are not cleanly or correctly presented. While the authors argue that their interpretation matches common implementation practice, the paper positions this analysis as a justification rather than an informal intuition, which requires higher rigor.

3. Although the empirical results are positive, the improvements are modest relative to the added architectural complexity, and the rebuttal does not fully change this balance.

Overall, while the rebuttal strengthens the empirical evidence, it does not sufficiently address the conceptual and theoretical weaknesses.

summary.value:
This paper proposes ConfSMoE, a Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) model designed to mitigate expert collapse and handle missing modalities.  
The method combines two components:
1. Confidence-guided gating (ConfNet): replaces softmax routing with a supervised "confidence" score aligned with ground-truth labels, avoiding gradient conflicts from entropy-based load-balancing losses.  
2. Two-stage imputation: imputes missing modalities first via intra-modality sampling (pre-imputation) and then refines them using sparse cross-attention over available modalities (post-imputation).  

The authors analyze the gradient cause of expert collapse, argue that load-balancing losses create conflicting gradients, and claim that confidence-guided routing both balances expert usage and improves robustness to incomplete multimodal data. Experiments on MIMIC-III/IV, CMU-MOSI, and CMU-MOSEI show moderate gains in F1/AUC over FuseMoE, FlexMoE, and other baselines.

strengths.value:
- Provides a clear gradient-based explanation of expert collapse and why load-balance losses cause conflicting updates.  
- Introduces a supervised confidence gate, which is a fresh idea compared to typical softmax or Laplacian routing.  
- Includes comprehensive experiments across clinical and multimodal benchmarks.  
- Visualization of expert usage and attention maps supports interpretability claims.

weaknesses.value:
- **W1. Unclear conceptual linkage between collapse mitigation and missing-modality imputation.**  
  The paper merges two largely independent problems--expert collapse (an optimization issue) and missing-modality imputation (a data-level issue)--without a convincing reason they must be solved together. Each part could stand as a separate paper, and the combined scope dilutes the narrative focus.

- **W2. Limited novelty of the two-stage imputation module.**  
  The "pre-imputation + cross-attention refinement" design closely resembles existing multimodal imputation methods like DrFuse [1], which also separate modality-specific and cross-modal reconstruction. The proposed variant adds little conceptual innovation beyond placing the procedure inside an MoE.  

- **W3. Empirical improvements are modest.**  
  Reported F1 scores (40-50 %) are low due to dataset imbalance, but even relative gains over baselines are small (1-4 %). Given the added architectural complexity, the empirical evidence feels insufficient to demonstrate clear practical benefit.

- **W4. Missing comparison to closely related gating approaches.**  
  The paper does not benchmark against recent load-balancing and uncertainty-aware routing methods that share similar motivations, such as Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing [2]. Without such baselines, the claimed advantages of the confidence-guided gate remain unverified.

- **W5. Reliance on supervised confidence limits generality.**  
  The gating network learns from ground-truth labels to estimate confidence, restricting applicability to supervised classification tasks. It is unclear how this method would extend to unsupervised or generative MoE settings where such supervision is unavailable.

[1] DrFuse: Learning Disentangled Representation for Clinical Multi-Modal Fusion with Missing Modality and Modal Inconsistency. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06197

[2] Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing Strategy for Mixture-of-Experts. https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15664

To provide precise reference, we have added FuseMoE [4] and the original Gaussian gating paper [5] to reference. We further provie expression and definition of all gaintg mechanism used in experiement in appendix.

    * We used the term "address" carefully and only claim for "mitigate" expert collapse. A direct evidence to claim "mitigate" is visualization of expert load as shown in appendix Figure 5, 6, 7. We consider Softmax router without load balance loss (Figure 5) produce clear expert collapse and Softmax router with load balance loss can achieve an idea balance load (Figure 7), which is common observation and aggreement in many existing literture [1,6,7,8,9]. ConfNet gating mechanism (Figure 6) showed clear pattern that distribute some load to those "less rich" expert as the training goes on. This may not be balanced as load balance loss as shown in Figure 7 since it is a hard load balance. But this hard balancing technique can cause significantly ambiguous expert selection. One heavy expert in one epoch tend to be largely suppressed in next epoch, leading to "Sharp Sinusoidal Wave" expert selection pattern. Although, we did not fully address expert collapse, but our proposed method can achieve relative good expert balance and smoother expert selection than load balance loss.



* **W5: Minor issues**

    Thank you for pointing this out. We have revised the typos in revision paper.



* **Q1: How sensitive is the performance to the accuracy of confidence supervision? Could miscalibrated confidence estimates lead to suboptimal expert routing?**

    We are happy to investigate the impact the miscali- and cali-brated confidence. By changing the temperature parameter of softmax in downstream task head, we can easily control the calibration of model. We use a wildly used metrics Expected Calibration Error (ECE) to measure how well the model is calibrated to actual accuracy. The ECE is closer to 0, the better the calibration is.  Please find the results in the following table: 
    
    | Metric | Temp=0.3 | Temp=0.6 | Temp=1 | Temp=2 | Temp=3 |
    | ------ | -------- | -------- | -------- |------- | -------- |
    | F1     | 43.62 $\pm$ 1.07 | 43.77 $\pm$ 0.94 | 44.35 $\pm$ 0.77 | 44.18 $\pm$ 0.11 |  43.08 $\pm$ 0.37 |  
    | AUC    | 69.75 $\pm$ 1.34 | 68.74 $\pm$ 0.38 | 70.41 $\pm$ 1.31  | 71.14 $\pm$ 0.61 |  69.22 $\pm$ 0.6 |
    | ECE (%)| 10.85 $\pm$ 1.72 | 8.61 $\pm$ 0.39 | 8.32 $\pm$ 1.27   | 6.34 $\pm$ 2.80 |  9.01 $\pm$ 0.96 | 

    Specifically, we set the temperature as 1 to indicate normal softmax, and large temperature value to make over-calibrated model and small temperature to make under-calibrated model. Both cases are not well-calibrated. We can clearly observed that temp = 2 is the best calibration setting and it is also the best performance in terms of AUC and comparable performance in F1 score. we can observed that worse calibrated confidence is definitely harmful to ConfNet as it is a true reflection of the instance contribution to downstream task. But the model performance is not very sensitive to calibration of model. A clearer trend is that better calibration may lead to better performance and vice versa.

## Rebuttal Summary

This paper introduces **ConfSMoE**, a confidence guided Sparse Mixture-of-Experts model designed to mitigate expert collapse and enhance robustness in multimodal learning with missing modalities. This work identifies that standard softmax routing and auxiliary load-balancing losses induce gradient conflicts and causes training difficulty, the authors propose a **Confidence-Guided Gating mechanism (ConfNet)**, a replacement of softmax with confidence scores aligned with ground-truth supervision, naturally balancing experts without the need for auxiliary losses. Additionally, the model incorporates a **Two-Stage Imputation strategy** that reconstructs missing data via modality sampling followed by sparse cross-modal attention refinement. Empirical evaluations on MIMIC-III/IV and CMU-MOSI/MOSEI demonstrate that ConfSMoE achieves superior stability and F1/AUC performance compared to most recent baseline under three different experimental setting. The behavior analysis of expert selecttion further indicate the strong match of theoretical analysis and emperical results.


We thank all reviewers recognizing our paper strength as the following: 


### Strength 1: Valuable and novel theoretical insights, accompanied by consistent empirical validation. (Reviewer dEKy, 8riB, q3sb)

This work reveals theoretical reason of expert collapse is first the extrem distribution of softmax, and show that the gradient generated by expert load-balance loss function can conflict with the gradient from learning a better gating scores, leading to difficulty in training MoE model. This gradient conflict can be emperically reflected from the expert-selection plot in appendix. The expert-selection plot often reflect a " Sharp Sinusoidal Wave" pattern, which experts that were heavily selected in one epoch tend to be suppresed in the next (Figure 7 in the paper). This oscillatory behavior indicates that the typical load balancing loss does not promote true specialization of expertise among experts but mearely enforces uniform usage, prioritizing balanced selecction over actual expert quality.



### Strength 2: Confidence-guided gating mechanism: A loss free solution to balance expert usage. (Reviewer dEKy, 8riB, q3sb)

We address this gradient conflict by a Confidence-guided gating function, where the gating score of expert depends on the downstream task confidence of each token. In other words, we replace the softmax gating score with downstream task confidence to achieve automatic load balance and remove gradient conflict. Intuitive, if an expert receive more token but lower confidence score, it will tend to be selected less by next step. This enables smoother expert balancing pattern than standard load balance loss (Figure 6 in the paper) and superior performance under both missing and complete modality setting.



### Strength 3: Effective Two-Stage modality imputation module. (Reviewer q3sb)

Unlike existing methods use shared representation of multimodal data to reconstruct, Two-Stage imputation module reconstructs missing modality by both modality-specific and instance-specific feature. This imputed modality preserved the characteristics of its original distribution without being significantly biased by other modality (see visualization on Figure 4 in the paper). This imputation strategy significantly increase the missing modality robustness under different missing ratio and shows superior performance over other missing modality imputation MoE. (Table 1, 2, and 7 to 13 in the paper)

summary.value: This paper introduces ConfSMoE, a confidence-guided sparse MoE designed to address the challenge of missing modalities in multimodal learning. Traditional SMoE models rely on softmax-based gating, which often causes expert collapse and poor generalization when inputs are incomplete. To overcome these limitations, ConfSMoE incorporates two key innovations: (1) it proposes a confidence-guided gating mechanism (ConfNet) that replaces softmax routing with token-level confidence scores, enabling stable and interpretable expert selection without requiring load-balancing losses; (2) it introduces a two-stage imputation strategy that reconstructs missing modalities through modality-specific inference followed by instance-level cross-modal refinement, preserving both structural and contextual fidelity. Experiments demonstrate that ConfSMoE outperforms existing methods in robustness and accuracy.

strengths.value:
1. This paper tackles a crucial problem in multimodal learning: how to effectively handle missing or incomplete modalities in real-world data. This challenge is highly relevant for domains such as healthcare, where data from different sensors or sources are often unavailable or corrupted.

2. The paper provides valuable insights into the root cause of expert collapse in SMoE models through a detailed gradient analysis, revealing that softmax-based gating and load-balancing losses induce conflicting optimization directions.

3. The proposed ConfSMoE framework has made contributions in both confidence-guided gating mechanism and the two-stage imputation strategy, where they demonstrated their unique advantages.

weaknesses.value:
The overall contribution of this paper is clear and nontrivial, so my comments on the weakness is relatively marginal.

1. Based on my understanding, the framework does not fully address temporal or causal dependencies among modalities or expert activations, which is a common problem in healthcare/activity monitoring/autonomous driving etc. The current design assumes static modality relationships and focuses primarily on handling missing inputs at the feature level. In dynamic settings such as time-evolving multimodal data or streaming environments, confidence-guided gating and two-stage imputation may not adapt quickly to changing modality relevance. So it is interesting to see further extension of this work on these settings.

2. Although the two-stage imputation is effective in handling inter-modality relationships, it may introduce additional computational overhead and stochasticity into the model training procedure.

Dear the authors,

Thanks for your great effort to provide a thorough response to my concerns, I really appreciate it. However, my concerns specified in the Weakness #3 still remain unsolved. In particular, in the original sparse MoE paper [1], their proposed TopK function is not continuous and, thus, sparse MoE equipped with that TopK function is not differentiable. 

I would like to emphasize that it is mathematically incorrect to apply the sum operator $\sum_{i}^{K}$ to indicate the TopK operator. I have suggested that you should provide a formal definition of the TopK function but I did not see it in the revised manuscript. 

Lastly, even the added definition of softmax router in the revised manuscript is not correct. In particular, as you define $u=W_rh$, where $h\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, so the dimension of $W_r$ should be $N\times d$, not $d\times N$. Then, $u$ should be an $N$-dimensional vector and, thus, the denominator of the softmax router should be defined as $\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(u_{j})$ rather than $\sum_{j}^{d}\exp(u_{j\neq i})$.

Given the above technical issues, I encourage the authors to revise the manuscript more carefully before submitting again. I think the current rating of 4 is reasonable. Therefore, I decided to keep it unchanged.

[1] Noam Shazeer, Azalia Mirhoseini, Krzysztof Maziarz, Andy Davis, Quoc Le, Geoffrey Hinton, and Jeff Dean. Outrageously large neural networks: The sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer. In ICLR, 2017.

summary.value:
In this paper, the authors propose ConfSMoE, a new sparse mixture-of-experts (SMoE) architecture designed to robustly handle missing modalities in multimodal learning. The paper identifies two major limitations of existing SMoE models:

(i) poor robustness under incomplete modality conditions, and

(ii) conventional load-balancing losses exacerbate expert collapse issue (caused by softmax-based router) by introducing gradient conflicts during optimization.

To address these problems, the authors introduce two key innovations:

1. A confidence-guided gating mechanism (ConfNet) that replaces softmax gating with token-level confidence scores, thereby avoiding gradient conflicts and improving expert diversity without using load-balance losses.

2. A two-stage modality imputation framework that reconstructs missing modalities using intra-modality sampling followed by instance-specific refinement through sparse cross-modal attention.

Lastly, the authors perform several experiments across three missing-modality settings to demonstrate the robustness and generalization of the proposed ConfSMoE. Furthermore, an ablation study is also provided to verify the theoretical analysis.

strengths.value:
1. Originality: The confidence-guided gate is a promising alternative for softmax routing. It reduces the “rich-get-richer” feedback loop responsible for expert collapse while remaining interpretable and supervision-aligned.

2. Soundness: The paper provides theoretical derivation for illustrating the expert collapse and the gradient conflicts induced by existing load balancing losses.

3. Relevance: The problem of gating design for alleviatiing expert collapse and handling missing modalities is of interest.

weaknesses.value:
1. Dependence on supervision: ConfNet’s confidence gating relies on supervised signals (via MSE loss to ground-truth confidence). This limits applicability to unsupervised or weakly labeled multimodal scenarios.

2. Training complexity and cost: The two-stage imputation introduces additional sampling and sparse cross-attention steps that may increase training time. Although Table 14 discusses FLOPs, a clearer runtime or memory comparison would strengthen claims of efficiency.

3. Quality: The theoretical analysis in Section 2 is not good. 

- Firstly, in Section 2.1, the MoE in Eq. (1) is not defined well. In particular, the explicit form of softmax router $G(\textbf{h})$ is not provided. Furthermore, how the top-K experts are selected is not specified, either. 

- Secondly, it seems that the Jacobian in Eq. (2) does not take into account the Top-K function. Additionally, sparse MoE is not differentiable in general due to the discontinuity of the Top-K function. Therefore, I'm quite concerned about the validity of Eq. (2).

- Thirdly, the Jacobian of softmax is not accurate. More specifically, softmax weights in MoE should depend on the input $\textbf{h}$ but the input is not considered when calculating the Jacobian. 

4. Clarity: 

- The maths presented in Section 3.2 is not rigorous and difficult to follow. In line 273, the notation $M_{m,i}$ is not defined precisely.

- The Gaussian gating is discussed in the paper but the authors do not provide any math formulation or reference for that gating. 

- The authors argue that the ConfSMoE helps address the expert collapse but there are not any evidences provided in the paper.

5. Minor issues:

- In line 205, "Confidence-Guidede"

- In Eq. (5), $\sum^{D}y_t\log(p_t)$

1. How sensitive is the performance to the accuracy of confidence supervision? Could miscalibrated confidence estimates lead to suboptimal expert routing?

2. Can the proposed ConfNet be adapted to unsupervised or self-supervised settings where no ground-truth confidence is available?

3. How significant is the additional computational overhead introduced by the two-stage imputation compared to FuseMoE or FlexMoE?

comment.value:
We thank the Reviewer dEKy spending time and effort to review our work and provide valuable comments. We wish the following reponse can address your concerns: 


* **W1: Unclear conceptual linkage between collapse mitigation and missing-modailty imputation.**


    Conceptually, when a modality is missing, the input signal to a standard softmax-based gating network is partial, producing unreliable representations for gating score learning (Eq. 3). Traditional softmax gating always produces high gating scores for the selected expert due to the natural exponential function of softmax even if the input signal is unreliable. This is counterintuitive: an unreliable modality representation receives a high gating score. The model will propagate this error during training: it always produces strong gating scores no matter the quality of the modality representation. This leads to worse expert collapse and thus worse performance and unreliable routing.

    ConfNet gating mechanism, however, measures the input signal’s downstream task confidence. When the input signal is unreliable, the confidence score will be relatively small for the downstream task. We take this low confidence score as the gating score to select experts such that the output of the selected expert will contribute less to the final representation from this unreliable signal. Therefore, the router will tend to select other experts for better representation learning for the next round, leading to a natural balance of expert load. Our two-modality imputation here is to reconstruct the missing modality to guide the routing process with the confidence score to learn better gating scores w.r.t. the quality of representation.

    In addition, the key characteristic of post-imputation is to integrate the “opinion” from different experts, which brings better imputation capability than a single model and this is also the key difference compared to other single-model imputation.

* **W2: Limited novelty of the two-stage imputation module**


    We would like to clarify that the idea is technically and conceptionally different to ours. DrFuse simply use the share representation between two mdoalities to impute the missing modality data, similar to ShaSpec. This imputation is trivial and ignore the modality-specific feature as we have discussed in Figure 1 (b). In addition, DrFuse introduced five different loss to achieve missing modality modelling, which may lead to difficulty of convergence and hand-craft parameter tuning. This design can be worse when more modalities are presented. My biggest concerns to DrFuse is that the design may lead to Pareto optimal solutions [1,2,3] as too many loss functions are introduced, stating that no signal objective can be improved without worsening at least one other objective. We believe that this Pareto optimal solution can be worse when more modality get involved, leading to suboptimal solution.

    Our design is novel since we consider the modality-specific feature and integrate the opinion of expert for instance-specific feature to fully impute the missing modality instead of inserting the imputation module to MoE. This is technically and conceptionally different to DrFuse and makes our tow-stage imputation outperform others. 



* **W3: Empirical improvements are modest**


    Compared to most recent works for missing modality modelling with MoE architecture, FuseMoE [4] and FlexMoE [5] in Neurips 2024 Splotlight, under the same experimental setting, FuseMoE improves other baseline in range [0.5%, 2%] in terms of F1 and FlexMoE improves in range [0%, 3%]. Our proposed method outperforms other baseline in range [1%, 4%] which can be considered as strong performance improvement in this particular task. Apart from improvement, we also proposed different kind of missing modality scenario as in Experiment II and III. Ours are all wins and shows smaller performance variance and stronger missingness resistence than other baseline. Please refers to our appendix Table 7 to 13.

* **W2: The two-stage imputation introduces additional sampling and sparse cross-attention steps that may increase training time. Although Table 14 discusses FLOPs, a clearer runtime or memory comparison would strengthen claims of efficiency. / How significant is the additional computational overhead introduced by the two-stage imputation compared to FuseMoE or FlexMoE?**


    We acknowledge that the pose-imputation can increase training cost under the same hyperparameter (e.g. number of layers, hidden size, number of head). However, the training time depends on many factors such as data parallel and programming efficiency. FlexMoE follows fastmoe[10] library to accelerate MoE forward by data parallel, this is the reason that we show FLOPs as complexity metrics as this is gives actual operation counts on floating-point operations. Furthermore, we did not adapt our approach on fastmoe as it does not allow us to control the behavior of gating score and integrate with our post-imputation. Thus, we do not have any data parallel implementation in our intial implementation. Therefore, we show how much computational cost wtih and without post-imputation, and will revise our implementation to the data parallel version implementation afterward. To be specific, we implement the same experimental setting as in Table 14 in Medium size model and the train/test time is calculated with 32 batch size per step.


    | Metric | FuseMoE | FlexMoE | ConfNet w/ post-imputation | ConfNet w/o post-imputation|
    | ------ | ---- |------- | ---- |------- |
    | Train Time (ms / step) | 24  | 15  | 30  | 20  |
    | Inference Time (ms / step) | 20 | 12  | 26  | 15 |
    | MFLOPs | 286.02 | 263.94 | 268.62 | 241.33 |
    | #Params | 11,524,392 | 11,371,473 | 11,330,062 | 11,300,304 |
    | Train Ave Mem (MB) | 2700 | 2400 | 2700 | 2000 |

    We can see that the post-computation indeed brings additional computational cost, but the complexity still remains at the same level as FuseMoE, which is acceptable for the performance gains.


* **W3: Quality of theoretical analysis in Section 2:**

    * Please find the expression for softmax gating function $G(h) = \frac{exp(u_i)}{\sum_j^d exp (u_{j})}$, where $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{W}_{r} \mathbf{h}$. We define the input of softmax gating as gating logits as $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ in line 140. Top-K routing, is to route the samples/tokens to those expert with first K biggest routing probability $g_i$ to feedforward process.
    * We argue that the statement: "Sparse MoE is not differentiable in general". Rigorously, Sparse MoE is not fully-differentiable, which means the model is differentiable on those selected/activated experts [1,2,3]. Eq. 3 is expression for router since it is the interests of analysis, we have applied ($\sum^K_i$) to indicate Top-K operation. To the level of router, the Jacobian of the model will be the summation of all K activated experts. Therefore, the expression rigorously holds already. Thank you for pointing this out. We will add additional description for this.
    * In line 140, we define the input of softmax gating as gating logits as $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. Therefore, we keep this notation for the derivation of Jacobian of Softmax gating in appendix and the derivation only need the logits of router $\mathbf{u}$. This gating logits is obtained from a linear mapping of representation $\mathbf{W}_{r} \mathbf{h}$, where $\mathbf{W}_{r} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times N}$ is gating weight. We will modify this accordingly in the revision version.
